## Eric’s Questions

1. We’re booking calls but closed nothing in six weeks. When you see that pattern, is it a lead-quality problem, a message problem, or an offer problem, and how do you tell them apart?

2. Our offer is a $9K–$15K transformation program from a new brand. Is our promise too big for the trust we’ve built? Would a smaller, concrete first offer close faster?

3. What’s the smallest, easiest-to-say-yes-to offer you think we could actually sell to a med spa this month?

4. If we lead with ads and move consulting to an upsell, what does the pricing and delivery actually look like? Walk us through a real example.

5. At an ads-led price point, what should the monthly retainer be, and how many clients would we need to cover our burn?

6. Once we simplify the offer, what should our real differentiation be? Is the fact that we’ve actually operated and managed inside med spas enough to win on?

7. We have almost no case studies. What’s the fastest ethical way to build proof: pilot pricing, a stronger guarantee, or taking on a first client at cost?

8. Would you take a med spa client at a steep discount right now purely to generate a real result and testimonial? Is that smart, or does it anchor us too low?

9. We’re currently on Meta and considering adding Google. Given our cash position, where should the next dollar go?

10. What cost per booked call should we realistically expect in the med spa market?

11. How much monthly ad spend do we need to know within 30 days whether this works?

12. If you were in our seat, with $150K invested, $28.5K in revenue, and cash running low, what specifically would you do in the next 30 days?

13. What’s the one metric you’d watch to decide whether this is working or whether we stop?

14. Realistically, how long should it take to reach consistent revenue if we execute your plan well: weeks or months?

15. What can we do that costs almost nothing and could realistically produce a client in the next 30 days?

## Jacques’ Questions

1. Which ad formats are working best right now?

2. What funnel approaches are working best right now?

3. How do you streamline the creative creation, approval, and review process with clients?

4. What SOPs do you recommend for managing outsourced suppliers and contractors?

5. Have you gotten lead magnets to work effectively? If so, what types and how are you using them?

6. Have you tested the “reverse lead magnet” approach from Lead Gen Jay? If so, has it worked, and how would you structure it for our market?

TAKE ALL THESE QUESTIONS AND OUT THEM IN 1 THROUGH HOWEVER MANY BUT JUST LIST THEM OUT TAEK ALL THE OTHER BABALE OUT: THE LUXORA COLLECTIVE
Business Assessment & Coaching-Session Prep
Prepared for Bethany  ·  Ahead of the session with Gill  ·  July 2026


Bethany — this is in two parts. Part 1 is an honest read on where TLC stands right now, so we walk in with the same picture. Part 2 is a focused list of questions to put to Gill — built to get specific, useful answers instead of general encouragement. Bring Part 2 into the room; Part 1 is our shared context.


PART 1
Where TLC Actually Stands
The numbers, stated plainly
Ten months in, roughly $150K invested against $28.5K revenue YTD. Six weeks of live outreach with sales calls booked but no client landed, and cash is running low. That combination isn't a "we're almost there" pattern — it's the market telling us something specific, and it's worth hearing clearly rather than pushing through.
The honest read: this is a demand and conversion problem, not an effort problem. Calls are being booked — so the top of the funnel works. Nothing is closing — so the issue lives in the offer and the trust behind it, not in how hard the team is working. That's actually good news, because offer and positioning are fixable in weeks; a broken team is not.
What's genuinely working (don't lose this)
A dedicated, capable team that shows up and executes. This is the hardest thing to build and you already have it.
Compass — a real infrastructure advantage. Most agencies our size run on scattered spreadsheets. We have a purpose-built sales platform with a shared prospect pool, claim-before-you-work discipline, forced pipeline hygiene (Keep-or-Kill, 45-day auto-release), call-transcript capture, and an AI "Council" that researches every spa before we dial. That is a legitimate edge.
Deep operational credibility in the space. Bethany has actually run med spas and managed the physicians inside them. Almost no competing agency can say that — and we are currently under-using it.
Disciplined process thinking. The KPI framework and setter/closer structure are more rigorous than most shops ever build.
What this tells us
The machine is well-built. The problem isn't the engine — it's what we're asking the market to buy. When execution is this disciplined and results still aren't coming, the finger points hard at the offer.

What isn't working — the brutal truth
The offer asks for maximum trust with minimum proof. We're asking a skeptical med spa owner to believe a brand-new agency will fix their ads, front desk, pricing, retention, and operations — for $9K–$15K, with a 2x guarantee — on the strength of one testimonial. The bigger the promise, the more proof a buyer needs. We've inverted that.
We're leading with the commodity and burying the moat. The website leads with "we build a profit machine" (generic, every agency says it) and hides the one unfair advantage: an operator who has actually run these businesses. We're selling the copyable thing and hiding the un-copyable thing.
The promise is too broad to say yes to quickly. "We install a growth engine and multiply your lifetime value" earns a "let me think about it." "We run your ads and book you consults" earns a yes. Breadth is killing the close.
No proof engine yet. Almost no case studies. Every sale is uphill until we manufacture a few undeniable results.
The channel questions — answered directly
Google Ads — yes, add it. The instinct is right. A med spa owner typing "med spa marketing agency" into Google is raising their hand; Meta interrupts people, Google captures existing intent. Run them together.
Traditional SEO — not right now. SEO is a 6–12 month payoff, and we're measuring runway in weeks. It's the wrong tool for a cash crunch. (There's a smarter, faster version of "search visibility" — that's covered in the separate note.)
The "just run ads, drop the consulting" idea — handle with care. The instinct to narrow the offer is correct. But pivoting to be a generic ad-management shop points us straight into the part of this industry that AI is compressing fastest — the platforms (Meta, Google) now auto-build and auto-run campaigns themselves. The fix isn't "drop what makes us different." It's "narrow the offer AND lead with the operator credibility that AI and generic agencies can't copy."
The one-line version of the whole assessment
TLC's problem was never the channel or the team. It's that we positioned ourselves as the commoditized thing (broad agency) while sitting on the defensible thing (med-spa operator expertise) — and never led with it. Narrow the offer, lead with Bethany's credibility, use our tools to run lean, and land a few undeniable results. That's the turn.

OPERATIONAL PRIORITY
Use Compass — Now, and Every Day
One thing that should change this week, independent of anything Gill says: the whole team needs to be living inside Compass. We paid to build it, it's genuinely good, and a tool only pays off if it's used consistently by everyone — not opened occasionally by some of us.
With cash tight and nothing closing, Compass is the single highest-leverage thing we already own. It costs us nothing more to run, and it attacks our actual problem — turning booked calls into closed clients.
What consistent Compass use buys us
Better calls, not just more calls. The AI Council researches each spa before we dial, so every conversation starts warm and specific. That's the fix for a booking-but-not-closing problem.
A pipeline we can trust. Claim-before-you-work, Keep-or-Kill, and the 45-day auto-release keep it honest — no stale deals hiding, no two people working the same spa.
Every call captured and learned from. Transcript capture means we stop losing what was said and can see why calls stall — which is how we fix the close rate instead of guessing.
Real numbers for the go/no-go. Compass's KPI tracking feeds an honest, bottom-up read on whether this is working. We can't decide clearly in a few weeks if the data isn't being logged now.
The ask for the team
Every prospect, every call, every outcome goes into Compass — starting now, no exceptions. If it's not in Compass, it didn't happen. The tool is only worth what we built it for if all of us use it the same way, every day. This is the cheapest, fastest performance upgrade we have — and it's already paid for.


PART 2
Questions for Gill
These are grouped so you can steer toward decisions, not vibes. The goal is to pull specifics out of him — real numbers, real timelines, a real 30-day plan. Watch for advice that quietly requires spending more cash we don't have.
On the offer & the no-close problem
We're booking calls but closed nothing in six weeks. When you see that pattern, is it a lead-quality problem, a message problem, or an offer problem — and how do you tell them apart?
Our offer is a $9–15K transformation program from a new brand. Is our promise too big for the trust we've built? Would a smaller, concrete first offer close faster?
What's the smallest, easiest-to-say-yes-to offer you think we could actually sell to a med spa this month?
On narrowing the offer
If we lead with ads and move consulting to an upsell, what does the pricing and delivery actually look like? Walk us through a real example.
At an ads-led price point, what's the monthly retainer, and how many clients do we need to cover our burn?
Once we simplify, what's our real differentiation — and is "we've actually operated med spas" enough to win on?
On proof & trust (the real blocker)
We have almost no case studies. What's the fastest ethical way to build proof — pilot pricing, a stronger guarantee, a first client at cost?
Would you take a med spa client at a steep discount right now purely to generate a real result and testimonial? Smart, or does it anchor us too low?
On the channels
We're on Meta and adding Google. Given our cash position, where should the next dollar go — and what cost-per-booked-call should we realistically expect in med spa?
How much monthly ad spend do we need to know, within 30 days, whether this works?
The go / no-go questions (most important)
If you were in our seat — $150K in, $28.5K revenue, cash running low — what specifically would you do in the next 30 days?
What's the one metric you'd watch to decide whether this is working or whether we stop?
Realistically, how long until consistent revenue if we execute your plan well — weeks or months? (We'll check that against our actual runway.)
The trap to watch for
Notice whether Gill's advice would require spending more money we're low on. If his plan needs another $10K of runway we don't have, that's not a plan — it's a bet. So end with this: What can we do that costs almost nothing and could produce a client in 30 days? His answer tells us the most about whether he's actually useful to us right now.



Come back from the session with what Gill says, plus our real runway number. That's what we build the go/no-go decision on together.  FROMJAQUES: Ad formats
Best funnel approaches
How they streamline the creative creation/review process with their clients.
